Note · Helmer — 7 Powers

4 min read867 wordsUpdated 2026-06-06notes/canon/canon-helmer-7-powers.md

Canon · Cluster: Landscape & Competitive Awareness · Maps to Course 04 (Competitive Strategy), Course 12 (Capstone)

  • Source: Hamilton Helmer, 7 Powers: The Foundations of Business Strategy (2016)
  • Core claim: There are exactly seven sources of durable competitive advantage. Most claimed "advantages" don't survive the test — if you can't name which power you have or are building, you probably don't have one.
  • Framework — the 7 Powers: 1. Scale economies — unit cost falls with volume. 2. Network economies — value rises with number of users. 3. Counter-positioning — you adopt a model the incumbent can't copy without damaging their existing business (the deepest and most overlooked power). 4. Switching costs — customers face loss/friction from leaving. 5. Branding — a justified perception of quality that supports pricing power. 6. Cornered resource — exclusive access to a valuable input (a patent, a key person, a deposit). 7. Process power — embedded organizational capability that can't be copied quickly (e.g. Toyota).
  • A real power = a Benefit (it improves your economics) that persists (a Barrier the competitor can't or won't cross). Helmer's rigor is the Barrier test.
  • Applies when: stress-testing any strategy or moat claim — "how will we win" (from canon lafley martin playing to win) must resolve to one of these seven or it's a wish.
  • Breaks when: the taxonomy is a static classification, not a playbook — it tells you what a power is, not how to originate one (Helmer's "invention" stage is thin). Powers can also erode (yesterday's network effect undone by multi-homing) — durability is relative, not absolute. And counter-positioning, the prized power, is the hardest to recognize before it's obvious. Sharper successor to Porter's generic strategies (canon porter competitive strategy).
  • Practitioner counterpoint: (researched 2026-06-05 — r/strategy corpus + Lenny's Podcast/Business Architect transcripts) The corpus confirms the discipline's real value is forcing you to name the specific barrier — Helmer's own framing on Lenny's Podcast is the practitioner antidote to lazy moat claims: "in a lot of decks it's like 'oh we have the most amazing team, we move the fastest'… you're on a treadmill, and if you stop running that treadmill you get creamed — but it's not power. The things that drive operational excellence can be mimicked." But r/strategy practitioners push back on applying it: the most-upvoted threads aren't about taxonomy at all — "Most organizations don't need a new strategy" (45↑) argues the real failure mode is execution and alignment, not a missing power ("the strategy isn't broken — the communication and ownership are"), and an MBA-bound poster asking "Which of these books is good for corporate strategy?" (34↑) gets pointed back to Porter, not Helmer. The taxonomy wins arguments; it doesn't run the offsite.
  • Researched layer (2026-06-05)
  • Canonical explanation (sourced): Helmer reduces strategy to one equation — "power requires a benefit and a barrier… [Buffett] is taking care of the benefit part by saying a castle — you have to have a pretty good understanding of why it's a castle and not a shack" (Lenny's Podcast). The Barrier is the whole game: a benefit competitors can copy is just a treadmill. The Business Architect explainer sharpens the same point — without a structural barrier, "competitive arbitrage" relentlessly copies your innovation "until your profit margins completely vanish."
  • Real application (mined): Helmer's own worked example — Netflix's scale economies: content is "a very large fixed cost, about 50% of their cost structure… they spread that fixed cost over more subscribers, so their cost per subscriber is less" than a smaller rival's. Contrast the non-power: when Blockbuster finally launched mail-order DVDs, "you couldn't tell it different from Netflix — they just copied it," proving UI/operational cleverness was mimicable, not a moat. He also stresses the powers are sequenced: nearly every startup "starts with counter-positioning," the one refuge from an incumbent who already has the capabilities to extend into your space.
  • Where the corpus pushes back on the book: practitioners treat 7 Powers as a diagnostic checklist, not an operating plan. r/strategy's recurring complaint is that org performance problems are misdiagnosed as strategy problems ("Most organizations don't need a new strategy," 45↑) — and the book is silent on the origination and execution work that actually builds a barrier, exactly the "invention stage is thin" gap noted above.
  • Sources in corpus: Lenny's Podcast — "Business strategy with Hamilton Helmer (author of 7 Powers)" (youtube.com/watch?v=hKq1_KPSqy0) · The Business Architect — "Deconstructing Hamilton Helmer's 7 Powers" (youtube.com/watch?v=2tiQrNtTzPA) · r/strategy "Most organizations don't need a new strategy" (45↑), "Which of these books is good for corporate strategy?" (34↑), "Playing to Win: How Strategy Really Works (one paragraph review)" (102↑).

Rep

Take one company you admire. Name its single strongest power from the seven — and the specific barrier that stops competitors from copying it. If you can't name the barrier, it's not a power.
